objectives: Define a Sufi using the chapter’s own wording.
Distinguish outward worship from inward intention and morality without separating them.
Discover how the chapter expresses an aim and its method (aims to … by + -ing) and keep a list of principles parallel.
Connect humility, generosity and kindness with observable actions rather than abstract labels.
content.pedagogy: Start from the text, not from a lecture on Sufism. Learners box the definition, then prove every idea with a quoted phrase. Grammar is discovered, not presented: You ask “What does a Sufi want? How?” and learners find that “by + -ing” answers “How?” before you name the rule.
priorKnowledge: “A person who …”, purpose with to + verb, and the difference between an example and a definition.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Do not reduce Sufism to poetry or imply that the text makes outward worship unimportant.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: aim + method (aims to … by + -ing) · parallel -ing list · in addition to + -ing · which-clause + helped + verb · is known as.
Notice (Activity 1): Board “A Sufi is a person who aims to get closer to Allah by following Islamic mysticism.” Ask only two questions: “What does a Sufi want?” and “How?” Pairs underline the answers and state the rule in their own words (by + -ing = the method) before you confirm it.
Build (Activities 2–3): learners repair the list of principles (… giving generously …, … not attaching importance …) and “In addition to being a Sufi”, then re-express the aim with (in order) to and “is known as” with “People know / regard … as …”.
Likely errors: *In addition to be · *not attach inside an -ing list · *helped developing.
Use (Activity 4): a 5–6 sentence description of a real person with at least one “by + -ing” and one parallel list.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Read the definition as one breath group with short pauses only before “who” and “by”: “a PERson | who AIMS to get CLOser to alLAH | by FOLlowing …”.
Word focus: Sufi (SOO-fee), MYS-ti-cism (four syllables), WOR-ship, BI-as-es.
In the list of principles, each -ing phrase rises slightly and the last one falls: “… wealth, status, and FAME↘”.
beforeReading: Show only the word “Sufi”. Pairs write one question they want the chapter to answer. Keep three questions on the board and treat every answer as a prediction until the text confirms it.
duringReading: First listening, books closed: Which of our questions was answered?
Box the formal definition.
Two columns: Outer practice / inner intention and morality, each with a quoted phrase.
Underline the sentence about Yunus’s contribution to Turkish.
afterReading: Complete the Quick Challenge with the definition in view.
Language Focus: Discover aim/method in Activity 1, then repair and rephrase in Activities 2–3.
Write five or six connected sentences about a real person’s role, aim and method.
Choose one principle from the chapter and state one realistic action that shows it.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook: “Sufi” on the board, pairs write one question for the chapter, three are kept on the board; 5–13 Listen with books closed for gist (which question was answered?), then read along and box the definition; 13–20 Pairs sort outer worship / inner intention and morality, every item with a quoted phrase, quick whole-class check; 20–24 Quick Challenge individually; 24–32 Language Focus: Activity 1 as whole-class discovery (What does a Sufi want? How?), Activities 2–3 in pairs while you monitor the -ing list; 32–38 Use: Learners draft five sentences about a teacher, artist or community figure (a person who … aims to … by …-ing), two volunteers read and the class names the aim and the method; 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: What belongs in the chapter’s definition of a Sufi?
How do outer and inner dimensions differ without becoming opposites?
Which moral principle is described through an observable action?
interactiveTips: Use the Sufism hotspot to confirm the outer/inner distinction.
Replay the moral-principles sentence and ask learners to count the -ing forms they hear.
Do not expand the definition with outside doctrinal detail.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give a three-part frame: “A Sufi is a person who ____. A Sufi aims to ____ by ____. One principle is ____.” Let learners copy the -ing forms from the text before they write their own.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write six connected sentences about a real person combining a definition, aim + method, one which-clause and a parallel list of three actions.

formativeAssessment: Defines from the source.
Keeps outer and inner dimensions distinct.
Uses “by + -ing” for method and keeps a list parallel.
expectedResponses: A Sufi aims to get closer to Allah by following Islamic mysticism; the chapter joins outward worship with inward intention and morality and presents Yunus as one of the first to write poems in simple Turkish.
content.transferTask: Choose one principle named in the chapter and describe one observable action that shows it.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners find the rule for “by + -ing” themselves before I confirmed it, and did they turn the value language into observable action?

classroomManagement.instructions: In pairs, sort the chapter into two columns: outer worship, and inner intention and morality. Add a quoted phrase to each item.
checkQuestions: What are the two columns? (outer worship, inner intention and morality)
What does each item need? (a quoted phrase)
classroomManagement.monitoring: Check that the definition of a Sufi is taken from the box in the text. In Activities 2–3, monitor the -ing list for parallel form. In the Use task, check by + -ing for method.

exitTicket: Complete: “A Sufi is a person who aims to ____ by ____. One principle in the chapter is shown by ____.”

rubricLevels.secure: Defines a Sufi from the source.
Supports each point with a quoted phrase.
Uses aim to and by + -ing and keeps a list parallel.
Turns a value into an action we can see.
rubricLevels.notYet: Ask “What would we see this person do?”.

objectives: Explain why Yunus’s language is described as accessible without calling it artistically weak.
Preserve approximate dates and source-qualified education claims.
Notice how the writer shows reason, balance, continuing influence and source certainty.
Distinguish reported madrasa study from the chapter’s direct description of tekke learning.
content.pedagogy: Make certainty visible. Learners color-code what the writer states directly, what is approximate and what only “some sources” report. The language work grows out of this: Learners discover that “according to”, “around” and “some sources say” are the writer’s tools for honesty about evidence.
priorKnowledge: Because/because of; contrast with but; years and approximate numbers.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Do not turn “some sources say” or approximate dates into certainty, and do not equate plain language with weak literary quality.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: reason with due to + noun · balanced evaluation (neither too … nor too …) · combine A with B · help + person + base verb · still for a continuing influence · source stance (According to …, Some sources say that …, around + date) · but … also, which-clause and passive was taught.
Notice (Activity 1): learners match five phrases from the first paragraph with plain-English meanings. Then ask: “Which phrase gives a reason? Which one tells us the influence has not stopped?”
Build (Activities 2–3): Choose According to / around / say, then complete the madrasa–tekke lines with also, which, taught. After each item ask: “How sure is the writer here?”
Likely errors: *According historical sources · *Some sources says · *was teach · who for a place.
Use (Activity 4): a 5–6 sentence profile with one balanced evaluation, one approximate date and one source-qualified claim.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Say source frames as single units: “acCORDing to hisTORical SOURces | …”, “some SOURces SAY that | …”.
Balance with contrastive stress: “NEIther too SIMple | nor too COMplex”.
Dates: “around twelve forty to twelve forty-one”, “around thirteen twenty to thirteen twenty-one”.
Word focus: MAD-ra-sa, PER-sian (/ʒ/), sig-NIF-i-cant, IN-flu-ence.
beforeReading: Read three statements aloud: one certain, one approximate, one reported (for example about your own school). Learners show 1, 2 or 3 fingers: certain / approximate / reported. Ask which words helped them decide.
duringReading: Underline the reason his works reach many people.
Circle “around” in the dates.
Highlight “According to historical sources” and “Some sources say” in a second color.
Separate madrasa information from tekke learning.
afterReading: Complete the Quick Challenge while preserving source stance.
Language Focus: Match the phrases, then report history carefully and connect the two kinds of learning.
Write a five-sentence profile with one balanced evaluation, one approximate date and one attributed claim.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Certainty signals: Three statements read aloud, learners show certain / approximate / reported with fingers and name the signal word; 5–14 Listen for gist (Why do people love his works?), then read and color-code direct / approximate / reported information; 14–20 Pairs compare colors and justify each one with the signal word, then contrast madrasa and tekke in two lines; 20–24 Quick Challenge; 24–32 Language Focus: Activity 1 in pairs with a whole-class question (which phrase gives a reason?), Activities 2–3 individually with pair checking; 32–38 Use: A five-sentence profile of a writer or artist, partners check that no “around” or “some sources” has been deleted; 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Which statements are direct and which are source-qualified?
Why is plain language not the same as poor literary quality?
What changes when “some sources say” is removed?
interactiveTips: Replay the source-attribution sentence before learners answer biography questions.
Use the Education hotspot to compare madrasa and tekke information.
Reject rewrites that silently remove “around” or “some sources”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give frames: “Around ____, …”, “According to ____, …” and “Some sources say that ____.”
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a short biography of a real writer using four different stance devices and label how certain each sentence is.

formativeAssessment: Preserves approximation.
Attributes education claims accurately.
Uses a balanced evaluation without contradiction.
expectedResponses: His works combine literary quality with simple language; some sources report madrasa study, while the tekke is presented as a place of Sufi education under a sheikh.
content.transferTask: Rewrite one historical claim so that its source and certainty level are explicit.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners keep the uncertainty of the source instead of “improving” it into stronger claims?

classroomManagement.instructions: Color the chapter in three colors: direct, approximate and reported information. Then compare with your partner and justify each color with the signal word. Contrast madrasa and tekke in two lines.
checkQuestions: How many colors? (three)
How do you justify a color? (with the signal word)
classroomManagement.monitoring: Check that approximate dates keep words like around or about. Check that madrasa study is attributed to some sources. In the Use task, ask partners to check every certainty signal.

exitTicket: Write one approximate claim and one source-qualified claim about a person you know from history.

rubricLevels.secure: Keeps the source stance: certain, approximate or reported.
Keeps the qualification in a retelling.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give the retelling without the signal word and ask what is missing.

rubricLevels.secure: Writes a balanced evaluation without contradiction.
Writes a connected B1 profile.

objectives: Explain at least two distinct functions of tekkes from the chapter.
Connect those functions with the difficult historical context without claiming tekkes solved the crisis.
Notice that the first paragraph adds information and the second builds a cause-result chain.
Relate community support to a concrete helpful action.
content.pedagogy: The chapter has two paragraphs with two different jobs: The first adds functions of the tekkes, the second builds a chain of causes. A jigsaw makes this visible: Half the class becomes experts on each paragraph and teaches the other half. Learners then discover that the linking words themselves (furthermore, too, especially / weakened by, caused, because of) show the job of each paragraph.
priorKnowledge: Not only … but also; because of; past continuous.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Do not present tekkes as only places of private worship or suggest that Yunus caused the political crisis.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: adding (not only … also, furthermore, too, especially) · cause and result (weakened by, caused, because of + noun) · while + past continuous passive for an ongoing background (were still being felt) · past simple for the new event · cope with.
Notice (Activity 1): learners sort six chapter sentences into “adds more information” and “shows a cause or a result”, then say which words helped.
Build (Activities 2–3): Choose were still being felt / took place / cope with, then say the same cause in a new way (The Babai revolts weakened …, … because of the defeat).
Likely errors: *were still feeling (active instead of passive) · *cope these situations · *because the defeat.
Use (Activity 4): 5–6 sentences about a real community facing change, with one while-background sentence.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Pause after the background clause: “While the NEGative effects of these reVOLTS were still being FELT | the deFEAT at Kösedağ took PLACE”.
-ed endings: weakened /d/, helped /t/, faced /t/, improved /d/, trained /d/.
Word focus: CIR-cum-stan-ces, FUR-ther-more, es-PE-cial-ly, or-gan-i-ZA-tions.
beforeReading: Show the Tekkes hotspot image. Ask: “What could a place like this do for people in hard times?” Collect ideas in a mind map as predictions.
duringReading: Group A reads paragraph 1 and lists the functions of the tekkes.
Group B reads paragraph 2 and draws the cause-result chain.
Everyone underlines the while-sentence.
afterReading: Complete the Quick Challenge with one function and one context detail.
Language Focus: Sort adding vs cause sentences, then choose the background/event forms and rephrase the causes.
Compare two functions of a modern community institution without claiming it solves every problem.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook: Tekkes hotspot image, class mind map of predictions; 5–12 Whole-class listening, then split: Half the class studies paragraph 1 (functions), half paragraph 2 (cause chain); 12–20 Jigsaw: A–B pairs teach each other their paragraph with one quoted sentence each, then check the mind map against the text; 20–24 Quick Challenge; 24–32 Language Focus: Activity 1 in the same A–B pairs (they already know one paragraph each), Activities 2–3 individually; 32–38 Use: Pairs compare two functions of a modern community center, library or charity, one while-sentence required; 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Which tekke functions are explicitly stated?
What problems form the historical background?
What would be an unsupported claim about the effect of tekkes?
interactiveTips: Use the two hotspots as the two sides of the jigsaw: Tekkes / Anatolia.
Replay the while-sentence and ask which event was still going on and which one happened.
Keep Yunus’s training under Taptuk Emre separate from the wider political causes.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give two boxes (functions / problems) and the frames “Tekkes were not only ____. They were also ____.” and “While ____ were still ____, ____ took place.”
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a six-sentence explanation connecting three functions with two historical pressures using at least three different linking words.

formativeAssessment: Names more than one tekke function.
Keeps the historical crisis separate from Yunus’s agency.
Uses the while-background and a cause-result link accurately.
expectedResponses: Tekkes provided Sufi training, community support and a place for poetry, while Anatolia faced revolts, defeat, invasion and serious social problems.
content.transferTask: Compare two functions of one community institution without claiming it solves every social problem.
content.teacherReflection: Did the jigsaw help learners see the different job of each paragraph, and did they connect institution and context without exaggeration?

classroomManagement.instructions: Half the class studies paragraph 1, half studies paragraph 2. Then, in A–B pairs, teach your paragraph to your partner with one quoted sentence. Check the mind map against the text together.
checkQuestions: Which paragraph does A study? (paragraph 1, functions)
What do you teach with? (one quoted sentence)
classroomManagement.monitoring: Check that more than one tekke function is named. Check that the crisis is kept separate from what Yunus did. In the Use task, check one while-sentence.

exitTicket: Write one “not only … also” sentence and one while-background sentence about your town or school.

rubricLevels.secure: Names more than one tekke function with evidence.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give three headings: training, support, poetry.

rubricLevels.secure: Keeps the historical context accurate.
Uses adding and cause links accurately.
Applies the idea to today with care.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give the frame “Like a tekke, a … can …”.

objectives: Contrast the strong Seljuk period with the later decline using chapter evidence.
Explain how migration pressure, population growth and governance problems interact.
Use superlatives, however and cause-result structures without reducing the chapter to one cause.
Connect management decisions with social consequences.
content.pedagogy: A multi-cause history chapter needs time. Lesson 1 turns the text into a timeline and a simple “strength graph” of the Seljuk state, so learners see the high point and the decline. Lesson 2 opens the language: Learners discover how the writer marks the high point (the most …), the turn (however) and the causes (caused … to, failure to … worsened).
priorKnowledge: Historical sequence from Chapter 3; superlatives; cause and result.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Migration is not presented as the only cause, and the chapter does not connect Yunus personally with the invasion.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: If we …, we can … (inviting the reader) · the most + adjective for a high point · However for a turn · where-clause for a place · caused + person + to + verb · failure to + verb … worsened.
Notice (Activity 1): learners read the first sentence and decide what the writer is telling them with “If … can …”.
Build (Activities 2–3): Choose the most powerful and brilliant / However / where, then turn the causes around: … migrated because of the Mongol invasion, … got worse because he failed to manage ….
Likely errors: *the more powerful period · Therefore instead of However · *the land which Yunus lived · *caused people migrate.
Use (Activity 4): 5–6 sentences about how a place or institution changed, with one high point, one however and one cause-result chain.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Stress the turn: a clear pause and fall-rise on “HOWever, |”.
Superlatives: “the MOST POWerful and BRILliant PERiod”.
Names inside full sentences: Ala al-Din Kayqubad (a-la al-DEEN kay-qu-BAD), Kaykhusraw (kay-khus-RAW).
Word focus: MI-grate, WOR-sened (/d/), MED-i-ter-RA-ne-an.
beforeReading: Draw an empty graph on the board: x = time (1220 → 1250), y = strength of the Seljuk state. Ask learners to predict the shape of the line.
duringReading: Mark Ala al-Din Kayqubad I evidence as the high point.
Mark migration and population evidence as pressure.
Mark governance failure separately.
Draw arrows only where the text supports a relationship.
afterReading: Lesson 1: complete the Quick Challenge and write one bridge note naming two interacting causes.
Lesson 2: Language Focus on the “if” perspective, the high point, the turn and the causes.
Write a connected B1 explanation showing how poor management can worsen an existing pressure.
content.lessonPlan: Lesson 1 (40 min): 0–5 Predict the shape of the “strength graph” of the Seljuk state; 5–15 Listen and read, then correct the graph with evidence (1220–1237 high point, decline after 1237); 15–25 Groups of three build a cause map with three cards (Mongol invasion → migration, Turkmen population, poor governance) and label every arrow with a word from the text; 25–33 Gallery check: Groups compare maps and remove any arrow the text does not support; 33–37 Quick Challenge; 37–40 Bridge note: Two causes that worked together; Lesson 2 (40 min): 0–4 Retrieve the graph and cause map from memory; 4–16 Language Focus Activity 1 as whole-class discovery (What does “If … can …” invite us to do?), Activities 2–3 in pairs; 16–24 Focus on errors from Activities 2–3 on the board, learners explain each correction; 24–34 Use: A paragraph about a place or institution that changed (the most …, however, because of, caused … to); 34–38 Pairs peer-check with the rubric; 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: What changes between the strong reign and the later decline?
Which pressures interact rather than operate alone?
What evidence supports criticism of governance?
interactiveTips: Use the two hotspots to contrast Seljuk strength and Mongol pressure.
Require a label such as because of / caused / worsened for each arrow.
Do not let migration become a stand-alone explanation for all later chaos.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give a three-node cause chain with one pre-selected sentence for each node and the frame “____ was the most ____. However, ____.”
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write two alternative causal explanations and evaluate which one the chapter supports better.

formativeAssessment: Separates chronology from causation.
Uses at least two interacting causes.
Uses the most … and however accurately.
expectedResponses: The chapter presents a high point under Ala al-Din Kayqubad I followed by decline, and explains the chaos through interacting pressures rather than a single cause.
content.transferTask: Explain a neutral school example in which poor management worsens an existing pressure.
content.teacherReflection: Did the graph and the cause map keep the reasoning multi-causal instead of turning the chapter into a list of dates?

classroomManagement.instructions: Lesson 1: In groups of three, build a cause map with three cards. Label every arrow with a word from the text. Then compare maps in a gallery check and remove any arrow the text does not support.
checkQuestions: How many cause cards? (three)
What do you remove in the gallery check? (arrows the text does not support)
classroomManagement.monitoring: Check that the graph shows the high point (1220–1237) and the decline after 1237. Make sure groups use two causes that work together. In Lesson 2, listen for the most … and however.

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “because of” and one with “failure to … worsened …”.

rubricLevels.secure: Keeps the chronology accurate.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give the two dates on the graph.

rubricLevels.secure: Uses at least two interacting causes with evidence.
rubricLevels.notYet: Ask “What else worked with this cause?”.

rubricLevels.secure: Uses high point, turn and cause language.
Applies the lesson responsibly.
rubricLevels.notYet: Ask “Is this the text, or our view?”.

objectives: Keep the Babai revolt, the Mongol attack on Erzurum and Kösedağ as distinct events in sequence.
Explain human and political consequences without sensationalising violence.
Distinguish a past expectation (believed … would …) from what really happened.
Use because / because of, however, caused and thus to link events.
content.pedagogy: Lesson 1 is about order and place: Learners number events while listening and mark them on a simple map (Erzurum, Kösedağ, Sivas, Kayseri, Erzincan). Lesson 2 is about viewpoint and linking: Learners discover that “would save” reports what people hoped, not what happened, and that because / because of need different continuations. Violent details are acknowledged calmly and never acted out.
priorKnowledge: Chapter 4 background; past simple and past continuous.
anticipatedMisconceptions: The Babai revolt and Kösedağ are separate events; the “Babas” did not save the Turkmen. Keep violence factual.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: would for a future seen from the past (believed these leaders would save them) · because + clause vs because of + noun · However for an unexpected turn · cause + noun · Thus for a result · -ing clause for a consequence (…, leaving not a single stone standing).
Notice (Activity 1): “… they believed these leaders would save them.” Ask: “Did the leaders save them? How do you know from the text?”
Build (Activities 2–3): Complete the second paragraph with However / caused / Thus, then correct because / because of and the -ing clause.
Likely errors: *Because many problems · *because of they believed · *made deep sorrow · *…, left not a single stone.
Use (Activity 4): 5–6 sentences explaining a difficult situation, what people expected and what really happened.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Keep the reported expectation together: “they beLIEVED | these LEADers would SAVE them”.
Sequence markers with a pause: “HOWever, |”, “FInally, |”, “THUS, |”, “AFter THAT, |”.
Numbers and places: “in twelve forty-two”, “in twelve forty-three”, “eighty kilometres northeast of Sivas”.
Word focus: re-TREAT, SOR-row, RAID-ed (/ɪd/). Keep a calm, even voice in the sentences about destruction.
beforeReading: Give three event cards—Babai revolt / Mongols capture Erzurum / battle of Kösedağ—and ask learners to predict their order only.
duringReading: Number the events while listening.
Mark the places on a simple outline map.
Underline “believed … would …” and label it “expectation”.
Use a second row for fear, sorrow and destruction.
afterReading: Lesson 1: complete the Quick Challenge using the event line and leave a bridge sentence naming one consequence.
Lesson 2: Language Focus on expectation, the unexpected turn and consequence.
Write a calm, neutral account that separates an event from its human consequence.
content.lessonPlan: Lesson 1 (40 min): 0–5 Predict the order of three event cards; 5–15 Listen with books closed and number the events, then read to check; 15–25 Map task in pairs: mark Erzurum, Kösedağ, Sivas, Kayseri and Erzincan with the year and one verb from the text; 25–32 Expectation vs reality T-chart: “They believed …” / “In the end …”, with evidence; 32–37 Quick Challenge; 37–40 Bridge sentence naming one consequence; Lesson 2 (40 min): 0–4 Retrieve the map orally; 4–12 Language Focus Activity 1 as whole-class discovery (Did the leaders save them?); 12–22 Activities 2–3 in pairs, then learners explain the difference between because and because of with their own examples; 22–33 Use: A calm “chronicle” of a real or school event (because …, however, caused, thus), no dramatic language; 33–38 Peer check: Underline every linker and check that each expectation is marked as an expectation; 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Which events must not be merged?
Which statement is an expectation rather than an outcome?
How can we describe destruction accurately without dramatic expansion?
interactiveTips: Use the Kösedağ hotspot only after the revolt/attack order is clear.
Replay the sentence with “believed … would” and ask whose view it is.
Do not ask learners to role-play attacks, threats or deaths.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Provide event cards and consequence cards to match, plus the frames “Because of ____, …” and “They believed that ____ would ____.”
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a seven-sentence account using five different sequence or consequence signals and one reported expectation.

formativeAssessment: Keeps events distinct.
Identifies the reported expectation.
Uses because / because of correctly and links consequences without sensationalism.
expectedResponses: The revolt was suppressed, the Mongols captured Erzurum in 1242, the Seljuks were defeated at Kösedağ in 1243, and the raids caused destruction and fear.
content.transferTask: Distinguish an event from its human consequences in a neutral example.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners keep event boundaries clear and separate what people hoped from what happened?

classroomManagement.instructions: Lesson 1: In pairs, mark Erzurum, Kösedağ, Sivas, Kayseri and Erzincan on the map. Add the year and one verb from the text. Then fill the T-chart: “They believed …” and “In the end …”.
checkQuestions: How many places? (five)
What are the two sides of the T-chart? (They believed, In the end)
classroomManagement.monitoring: Check that the events stay distinct. Make sure the expectation is attributed. Keep the tone calm and factual, without dramatic detail. In Lesson 2, listen for because and because of.

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “because” and one with “because of” about the same situation.

rubricLevels.secure: Keeps the events in order.
Separates the expectation from the outcome.
rubricLevels.notYet: Ask “What did they believe? What happened?”.

rubricLevels.secure: Uses because, because of and result links correctly.
Describes destruction calmly and without sensationalism.
rubricLevels.notYet: Ask “What does the text say exactly?”.

objectives: Trace the shift from raids to economic dependence, administrative control and direct attachment.
Discover why the chapter uses the passive and what it puts in focus.
Explain a change of status over time (in time … became, began to be …).
Analyse how political-economic systems affect ordinary people without treating one date as the whole story.
content.pedagogy: Lesson 1 handles the sensitive first paragraph calmly (the teacher reads it once, without lingering) and then builds a “staircase of dependence” from the second paragraph. Lesson 2 asks why so many sentences start with the people or lands that suffered: Learners sort active and passive sentences and discover that the passive keeps the victims in focus.
priorKnowledge: Chapter 5 consequences; was/were + past participle; comparatives.
anticipatedMisconceptions: The agreement did not restore full independence, and 1308 is not the beginning of all Mongol pressure.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: passive was/were + past participle to keep the affected side in focus · in time … became + adjective · almost like + noun · began to be + past participle · make + object + comparative (made … poorer).
Notice (Activity 1): learners sort six chapter sentences into “the subject acts” / “the action happens to the subject”. Ask: “Who is first in the passive sentences? Why does the writer put them first?”
Build (Activities 2–3): Choose became / almost like / to be sent, then say the same result with the people as subject (… became poorer) and the same action in the passive (Anatolia began to be administered by …).
Likely errors: *began to send (active) · *almost alike · *made the people more poor.
Use (Activity 4): 5–6 sentences about a person, group or organization that gradually loses control.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Passive verbs are usually unstressed: “the MEN were KILLED | by the SWORD” — “were” is weak (/wə/).
Stress the stages of change: “in TIME | the SELjuks beCAME dePENDent”, “beGAN to be SENT”, “DIrectly atTACHED”.
Dates: “after twelve seventy-seven”, “in thirteen oh-eight”.
Word focus: CAP-tive, ad-MIN-is-ter, de-PEN-dent, IL-khan-ate.
beforeReading: Ask learners to distinguish immediate human consequences from longer-term political and economic consequences with one neutral example (a storm: damaged houses today / higher prices next year).
duringReading: Mark the passive sentences about people and cities.
Build the staircase: agreement → dependence → tax sent every year → governors → direct attachment in 1308.
Circle words that show change over time.
afterReading: Lesson 1: Quick Challenge plus one bridge note naming the first and last step of the staircase.
Lesson 2: Language Focus on passive focus and change of status.
Build a neutral three-step chain showing how one pressure can deepen another, and say who is affected.

content.chapter: Chapter 7: Yunus as a Wise Dervish
objectives: Explain how the chapter places Yunus inside the historical crisis without making him a political solution.
Identify poetry as the chapter’s stated most influential tool.
Keep the Qur’an/Sunnah foundation distinct from the additional inspiration of earlier Sufis.
Use time, pressure and response language (during, under … pressure, in such an environment, helped people make sense of).
content.pedagogy: Build a context → response → foundation triangle on the board. Learners fill each corner with a quoted phrase. The last two sentences are the key: Learners discover that “comes from” names the foundation and “was also inspired by” adds a second influence, so the two are not equal.
priorKnowledge: Historical crisis from Chapters 4–6; past continuous for background.
anticipatedMisconceptions: The chapter does not say Yunus ended political conflict, and it does not separate his Sufi understanding from the Qur’an and Sunnah.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: foundation vs additional influence (comes from / was also inspired by) · parallel past continuous (were spreading … and establishing …) · influential among · help + person + base verb · During + noun · under … pressure · such an environment · his most influential tool.
Notice (Activity 1): learners read the last two sentences and decide how the two sources differ. Ask: “Which word tells us the second source is added?”
Build (Activities 2–3): correct establishing / among / make, then complete the first paragraph with During / under / such / most.
Likely errors: *were spreading … and established · *influential between · *helped people making · While + noun.
Use (Activity 4): 5–6 sentences about a person who responds to a need in a difficult time, ending with where their ideas come from.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Background frames as chunks: “DURing the SAME PERiod, |”, “under MONgol PRESSure”.
Contrast the two sources: “COMES from the QUR’an …” / “He was ALso inSPIRED by …”.
Word focus: DER-vish, in-flu-EN-tial, NO-mads, Tur-kes-TAN, Kho-ra-SAN.
beforeReading: Recall one social pressure from Chapters 4–6 and ask what kinds of non-material support people might look for in such times.
duringReading: Mark the context sentences.
Underline what Yunus actually does.
Box “most influential tool”.
Separate “comes from” from “was also inspired by”.
afterReading: Complete the Quick Challenge with the triangle visible.
Language Focus: Compare the two sources, correct the forms, then complete the time–pressure–response lines.
Explain how language or art may support reflection without claiming it removes material hardship.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Recall: One pressure from Chapters 4–6 in 30 seconds per pair, then “What else do people need in hard times besides food and safety?”; 5–13 Listen and read, then the triangle on the board: context / response / foundation; 13–20 Think-pair-share: Each pair fills one corner with a quoted phrase and defends it; 20–24 Quick Challenge; 24–32 Language Focus: Activity 1 as whole-class discovery (Which word shows the second source is added?), Activities 2–3 in pairs; 32–38 Use: A short profile of someone who helped others in a hard time, ending with “comes from … / was also inspired by …”, plus one sentence saying what they did not claim to solve; 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: What problem is Yunus shown responding to?
What does the text call his most influential tool?
How do “comes from” and “was also inspired by” differ?
interactiveTips: Use the Wise Sufi and Poetry hotspots to separate role from tool.
Replay the final paragraph for the foundation/inspiration wording.
Reject claims that poetry ended political conflict because the source does not say this.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Use three headings (Context / Response / Foundation) and the frame “His ideas come from ____. He was also inspired by ____.”
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a six-sentence source-safe profile including one limitation sentence about what poetry is not claimed to solve.

formativeAssessment: Connects Yunus to the context accurately.
Identifies poetry as the stated tool.
Separates foundation from inspiration.
expectedResponses: Yunus is presented as a traveling wise Sufi who helped people make sense of life with poetry; his understanding comes from the Qur’an and Sunnah and he was also inspired by earlier Muslim Sufis.
content.transferTask: Give one example of how language or art can help people reflect during difficulty without claiming it removes the material problem.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners qualify Yunus’s role and keep the foundation/inspiration distinction?

classroomManagement.instructions: In pairs, fill one corner of the triangle: context, response or foundation. Use a quoted phrase and defend it to the class.
checkQuestions: What are the three corners? (context, response, foundation)
What do you use? (a quoted phrase)
classroomManagement.monitoring: Check that poetry is named as Yunus’s tool. Check that the Qur’an and Sunnah are the foundation and earlier Sufis are an inspiration. In the Use task, listen for comes from and was also inspired by.

exitTicket: Complete: “His understanding comes from ____. He was also inspired by ____.”

rubricLevels.secure: Connects Yunus to the context accurately.
Gives evidence for his role and his tool.
Separates foundation from inspiration.
rubricLevels.notYet: Ask “Which comes first? Which is added?”.

rubricLevels.secure: Applies the profile to today with care.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give the frame “… helped others by …”.

objectives: Define tawhid exactly as the chapter does.
Distinguish the direct definition from viewpoints attributed to Yunus and to the theory named in the text.
Use definition (which means), attribution (according to), conclusion (so) and exclusive focus (only one …).
Discuss theological content with precise source boundaries and respectful wording.
content.pedagogy: Source attribution organises both lessons. Lesson 1 separates definition, attributed explanation and poem with three colored labels. Lesson 2 turns to language: Learners discover how “which means”, “according to” and “so” build a definition–viewpoint–conclusion chain, and how “only one …” and “nothing … except …” say the same idea in two ways. Learners are not asked to debate or extend theology beyond the text.
priorKnowledge: Definition vs attributed viewpoint from Chapters 1–2 and 7.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Do not reduce tawhid to social unity or strengthen an explanation beyond the chapter’s wording.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: meaning of key phrases (a vivid love, the source of all things, a key idea, an enemy to his own soul) · …, which means … · According to + person · So for a conclusion · exclusive focus (there is only one …, and that is … / the only … / nothing … except …).
Notice (Activity 1): learners match four phrases from the chapter and the poem with plain meanings.
Build (Activities 2–3): Complete the definition–viewpoint–conclusion chain with which / According to / So, then say “only one” in two other ways (Nothing is truly real except the Creator. Allah is the only true existence.).
Likely errors: Who for an idea · Due to instead of According to · But instead of So.
Use (Activity 4): 5–6 sentences explaining an important idea from school, science or community life from definition to conclusion.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Pause after the attribution so the viewpoint stays clearly owned: “acCORDing to YUnus EMre, | …”.
Read “there is ONly ONE true exISTence | and THAT is alLAH” calmly, without preaching intonation.
Word focus: TAW-hid, ONE-ness (/wʌn/), ex-IST-ence, U-ni-verse, VIV-id.
beforeReading: Prepare three labels: definition / attributed explanation / poem. Ask learners to predict where in the chapter each may appear.
duringReading: Box the definition of tawhid.
Underline every attribution phrase.
Mark the “so” conclusion.
Identify the “only one” statement and the “whoever” line in the poem.
afterReading: Lesson 1: Quick Challenge plus a bridge note containing one definition and one attributed statement.
Lesson 2: Language Focus on meaning, definition, attribution and exclusive focus.
Paraphrase one strong statement using “According to the chapter …” or another source-safe frame.
content.lessonPlan: Lesson 1 (40 min): 0–5 Three labels (definition / attributed explanation / poem): Predict their order in the chapter; 5–15 Listen and read; 15–26 Pairs color-code the chapter with the three labels and quote one sentence for each; 26–33 Read the poem together in meaning groups, learners say in simple words what each line claims, without extending it; 33–37 Quick Challenge; 37–40 Bridge note: One definition and one attributed statement; Lesson 2 (40 min): 0–4 Retrieve the color-coding; 4–14 Language Focus Activity 1 in pairs, then Activity 2 as whole-class discovery (which word defines, which reports a view, which concludes?); 14–22 Activity 3, then a “same idea, three ways” board with learners’ own paraphrases; 22–33 Use: A definition-to-conclusion paragraph about an important idea (for example fair play, recycling, friendship); 33–38 Source-boundary check: Partners mark any sentence that sounds more certain than its source; 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: What is directly defined?
Which explanation is attributed, and to whom?
What wording would make an attributed claim sound falsely certain?
interactiveTips: Use the Tawhid hotspot for the definition and the Unity hotspot for the attributed explanation.
Replay sentences beginning “According to …” before paraphrasing.
Do not turn the lesson into a theological debate beyond the text.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Color-code definition / according to / so and give one paraphrase frame: “____ is ____, which means ____. So ____.”
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a seven-sentence explanation using two different attribution frames and one “only …” statement, and label the definition sentence.

formativeAssessment: Defines tawhid from the source.
Attributes viewpoints correctly.
Uses exclusive-focus language without expanding the theology.
expectedResponses: The chapter defines tawhid as the Oneness of Allah and attributes further explanations about existence to Yunus Emre and to the theory of the unity of existence.
content.transferTask: Paraphrase one strong statement using source-safe language such as “According to the chapter …”.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners keep attribution visible and avoid turning interpretation into unqualified narrator fact?

classroomManagement.instructions: Lesson 1: In pairs, color-code the chapter with three labels: definition, attributed explanation and poem. Quote one sentence for each. Then read the poem in meaning groups and say what each line claims.
checkQuestions: How many labels? (three)
Do you extend the poem’s meaning? (no, only say what the line claims)
classroomManagement.monitoring: Check that tawhid is defined from the source. Make sure explanations are attributed to Yunus Emre or the unity of existence. Stop any expansion beyond the text. In Lesson 2, ask which word defines, which reports and which concludes.

exitTicket: Write one “…, which means …” sentence and one clearly attributed sentence.

rubricLevels.secure: Defines tawhid from the source.
Attributes each viewpoint correctly.
Uses definition, viewpoint and conclusion language.
Stays inside the source.

objectives: Keep worship/obedience and love of Creator and creation as distinct strands before connecting them.
Follow the chain of ideas in the first part of the chapter with its linking phrases.
Understand “should” in the poem as an expected duty and “those who … also …” as a two-way relationship.
Turn a stated principle into a concrete responsibility without inventing a new religious claim.
content.pedagogy: The chapter has two strands: The goal and the commands (worship and obedience) and, at the end, love of the Creator and the created. Learners find evidence for each strand before connecting them. The first Language Focus activity is itself a discovery task: Putting the sentences in order shows how “as a result of”, “in this way”, “the main goal” and “this unity” tie the ideas together.
priorKnowledge: Goal and purpose language; attributed religious content from Chapter 8.
anticipatedMisconceptions: The chapter does not say that prayer is its only moral concern or that loving creation is unrelated to loving the Creator.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: text cohesion (As a result of …, In this way, The main goal … is to …, this unity) · for + -ing for purpose · Anyone who … should … for an expected duty · the most important part · Those who …, and those who … also ….
Notice (Activity 1): learners order the sentences of the first part and explain which words helped (In this way points back, this unity points back).
Build (Activities 2–3): Decide what “should” expresses in the poem, then correct the superlative and the position of “also”.
Likely errors: *It is most important part · *love also the Creator · *those who loves.
Use (Activity 4): 5–6 sentences about a goal in school, teamwork or health and the responsibilities around it.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Goal and duty frames: “the MAIN GOAL for HUmans | is to REACH …”, “ANyone who CLAIMS … | should KNOW …”.
The mirror sentence at the end has a clear rhythm: “those who love the CreATor | love the creATed, | and those who love the creATed | ALso love the CreATor”.
Word focus: cre-A-tion, re-FLEC-tions, re-QUIRE-ments, CREA-ture.
beforeReading: Ask learners to predict whether the chapter will focus on worship, love or both, and keep the prediction open.
duringReading: Mark the goal statement.
Underline the duty language in the poem.
Mark the final Creator/created relationship separately.
afterReading: Complete the Quick Challenge.
Language Focus: Order the chain of ideas, interpret “should”, then correct the superlative and “also”.
Write a connected four- to five-sentence synthesis of both strands.
Write a neutral principle → responsibility transfer example.
content.lessonPlan: 0–4 Prediction: Worship, love or both?; 4–12 Listen and read, then two colors: Goal and commands / love; 12–18 Pairs find one quoted sentence for each strand and one word that connects them; 18–22 Quick Challenge; 22–31 Language Focus: Activity 1 first with paper strips on the desk (learners explain each link word), then on screen, Activities 2–3 in pairs; 31–38 Use: A goal-and-responsibility paragraph (The main goal of our team is to … . Anyone who … should … . Those who … also …); 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: What is presented as the main goal?
What responsibility appears in general form?
How does the closing love relationship connect with the commands without replacing them?
interactiveTips: Use the A Muslim’s Duties hotspot for the poem and the Love hotspot for the closing strand.
Keep the poem reading phrase by phrase and non-theatrical.
Require evidence before learners connect a value to the text.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Use two headings and the frames “The main goal is to ____.” and “Anyone who ____ should ____.”
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write six connected sentences linking both strands with result, goal, purpose and responsibility language.

formativeAssessment: Identifies both strands.
Explains how the link words connect the ideas.
Avoids turning personal transfer into source fact.
expectedResponses: The chapter moves from creation to the main goal of reaching unity with Allah, reminds us of His commands such as the five daily prayers, and ends with a two-way love between the Creator and the created.
content.transferTask: Write one neutral principle → responsibility example using goal and purpose language.
content.teacherReflection: Did the ordering task help learners see how the text is held together, and did they connect both strands without collapsing one into the other?

classroomManagement.instructions: Mark the chapter in two colors: goal and commands, and love. Then, in pairs, find one quoted sentence for each strand and one word that connects them.
checkQuestions: How many colors? (two)
What else do you find? (one word that connects them)
classroomManagement.monitoring: Check that both strands are found. In Activity 1, ask learners to explain each link word on the strips. In the Use task, check Anyone who … should and Those who … also.

exitTicket: Write one goal sentence and one “Anyone who … should …” sentence about your class.

rubricLevels.secure: Gives evidence for both strands.
Explains how the link words connect the ideas.
Writes a connected synthesis.
Keeps personal transfer separate from source facts.

objectives: Explain the chapter’s love → unity and harmony / absence of love → negative emotions contrast.
Interpret heart and throne language as figurative within the chapter.
Preserve the chapter’s positive treatment of intellect.
Use clarification (that is), interpretation (describe … as …), a that-clause and not only … but also ….
content.pedagogy: Separate conceptual prose from poetic image. Lesson 1 builds the love/result pairs and a literal-vs-figurative sort. Lesson 2 opens the language of explanation: Learners notice that the writer explains his own image with “that is”, interprets with “describe … as …” and adds intellect with “not only … but also …”, so heart and intellect are not rivals.
priorKnowledge: Literal and figurative meaning; cause and result.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Do not read throne/heart imagery as a physical description, and do not say the chapter rejects intellect.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: meaning of figurative phrases (the throne of the Lord, breaking a heart, both worlds, since eternity) · where … is absent, … arise (plural verb) · that is for clarification · describe A as B · the eye that sees … (that-clause) · not only … but also ….
Notice (Activity 1): learners match four phrases with plain meanings, then find the words the writer uses to explain his own image (that is).
Build (Activities 2–3): Choose arise / as / not only, then rebuild “The heart is the eye that sees the truth and the center of understanding.”
Likely errors: *emotions arises · *described it like · *emphasizes both heart but also intellect · the that-clause separated from its noun.
Use (Activity 4): 5–6 sentences about why a value matters in friendship, family or school life.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Clarification has its own tune: A pause and a lower voice on “| THAT is, | the PLACE where …”.
Contrastive stress: “NOT only HEART | but ALso INtellect”.
Read the poem in two halves with a pause at the semicolon; treat the image calmly, not theatrically.
Word focus: THRONE (/θ/), e-TER-ni-ty, HAR-mo-ny, IN-tel-lect.
beforeReading: Ask: “What does it mean to break someone’s heart?” Collect answers and show that the phrase is not about the body. This prepares literal vs figurative reading.
duringReading: Build love present / love absent result pairs.
Mark “that is” and “For this reason”.
Underline the poem image.
Box the sentence that values intellect.
afterReading: Lesson 1: Quick Challenge and a bridge note with one literal idea and one figurative image.
Lesson 2: Language Focus on meaning, explanation and addition.
Write a paragraph explaining one respectful action and its effect on another person’s feelings.
content.lessonPlan: Lesson 1 (40 min): 0–5 “Break someone’s heart” — literal or figurative?; 5–15 Listen and read; 15–25 Card sort in groups: Literal statements / figurative images (for example “Love brings unity and harmony” / “the throne of the Lord”); 25–32 Heart and intellect: Pairs find the evidence that intellect is also valued and write one balancing sentence; 32–37 Quick Challenge; 37–40 Bridge note; Lesson 2 (40 min): 0–4 Retrieve the card sort; 4–12 Language Focus Activity 1, then find the writer’s own explanation word (that is); 12–22 Activities 2–3 in pairs, then learners build one more “the … that …” sentence about a school object (the key that opens …); 22–33 Use: A paragraph about a value (where respect is absent, … / that is, … / not only … but also …); 33–38 Pairs read and give one “that is” clarification to each other’s paragraph; 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: What results are linked with the absence of love?
Which expression is figurative rather than physical?
What proves the chapter values intellect too?
interactiveTips: Use The Heart hotspot for the image and the Intellect hotspot to prevent a false heart-vs-intellect contrast.
Replay the “that is” and “For this reason” sentences and ask what job each one does.
Do not ask learners to invent theological meanings for the poem.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Use three labels (Literal idea / Figurative image / Intellect evidence) and the frame “Where ____ is absent, ____ arise.”
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a seven-sentence interpretation using “that is”, “describe … as …” and one “not only … but also …” structure.

formativeAssessment: Explains the image as figurative.
Preserves the intellect evidence.
Uses clarification and addition language coherently.
expectedResponses: Love brings unity and harmony; the heart is presented as the center of love and understanding, and intellect is also valued as “a light from Allah”.
content.transferTask: Describe one respectful action that protects another person’s feelings and explain its consequence.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners interpret the image from the text and avoid creating a false opposition between heart and intellect?

classroomManagement.instructions: Lesson 1: In groups, sort the cards into literal statements and figurative images. Then, in pairs, find the evidence that intellect is also valued and write one balancing sentence.
checkQuestions: What are the two groups? (literal, figurative)
What do you write? (one balancing sentence)
classroomManagement.monitoring: Check that “the throne of the Lord” is sorted as figurative. Check that pairs find “a light from Allah”. In Lesson 2, listen for that is and the … that ….

exitTicket: Write one literal chapter idea and one figurative image, then explain the difference with “that is”.

rubricLevels.secure: Explains the concepts with evidence.
rubricLevels.notYet: Point to “Love brings unity and harmony”.

rubricLevels.secure: Explains a figurative image without taking it literally.
rubricLevels.notYet: Ask “Is this a real place or a picture?”.

Applies the idea respectfully.

objectives: Explain how heart and intellect are presented as supporting one another.
Interpret remembering death as advice toward a meaningful life, not despair.
Distinguish the writer’s report of Yunus’s view, Yunus’s own poem and the words of the Prophet (pbuh).
Use for + person + to + verb, according to / reporting verbs, as … said and whoever / a person who.
content.pedagogy: Who is speaking? This question organises the chapter. Lesson 1 uses three colors for three voices (the writer reporting Yunus, Yunus’s poems, the Prophet’s saying) and keeps the theme calm. Lesson 2 shows how English marks these voices (He highlights that …, According to him, …, as … said:) and how a general statement is made (A person who … / Whoever …).
priorKnowledge: Heart and intellect from Chapter 10; attribution from Chapter 8.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Remembering death is not presented as despair, and intellect alone is not presented as guaranteeing salvation.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: voices in a text (He highlights that …, According to him, …, as the Prophet … said: “…”) · for + person + to + verb for a goal · must for necessity · A person who … / Whoever … for a general statement.
Notice (Activity 1): learners sort five parts of the chapter by voice and name the signal that shows each one.
Build (Activities 2–3): Turn “According to him” into a reporting verb (He believes that …) and “A person who …” into “Whoever …”, then choose to reach / as.
Likely errors: *for a person reaching · *Whoever who · although instead of as.
Use (Activity 4): 5–6 sentences about a principle for learning or friendship with one attributed view and one general statement.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Signal each voice with a pause: “acCORDing to HIM, | …”, “as the PROphet MuHAMmad (peace be upon him) SAID: | …”.
General statements: “WHOever COMES into this WORLD | must LAter LEAVE it”.
Keep a calm, even voice; stress the advice (meaningful, honest), not the fear.
Word focus: sal-VA-tion, IN-tel-lect, ad-VI-sor, MEAN-ing-ful.
beforeReading: Ask: “What makes advice different from a threat?” Collect two short examples (a coach’s advice / a warning sign).
duringReading: Mark the heart and intellect requirement.
Three colors: The writer reports Yunus / Yunus’s poem / the Prophet’s words.
Underline must and whoever.
Identify the explicit link to a meaningful and honest life.
afterReading: Lesson 1: Quick Challenge plus a bridge chart speaker → idea.
Lesson 2: Language Focus on voices, reporting and general statements.
Write a practical limited-time decision in neutral language, without fear-based framing.
content.lessonPlan: Lesson 1 (40 min): 0–5 Advice or threat? two quick examples; 5–15 Listen and read; 15–25 Three-color highlighting of voices in pairs, then a whole-class check with the signals (highlights that, according to him, as … said, quotation marks); 25–32 Heart and intellect: What must happen for salvation according to the text?; 32–37 Quick Challenge; 37–40 Bridge chart speaker → idea; Lesson 2 (40 min): 0–4 Retrieve the three voices; 4–12 Language Focus Activity 1 (the sort confirms Lesson 1); 12–22 Activities 2–3 in pairs, then learners report a classmate’s opinion with “She believes that …”; 22–33 Use: A principle paragraph for learning or friendship (For a student to …, … must … / According to … / Whoever …); 33–38 Pairs check that every view has an owner; 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: How do heart and intellect support one another?
Whose voice is being reported in each statement?
What wording shows that death is used as advice rather than despair?
interactiveTips: Use the two hotspots (Heart and Mind / Death as an Advisor) as related but distinct strands.
Replay the attribution sentences before learners generalise.
Do not dramatise death or use fear-inducing role-play.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Provide speaker labels and the frames “According to ____, …”, “For a person to ____, … must ____.” and “Whoever ____ ____.”
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write six source-aware sentences separating the quoted saying, Yunus’s view and a neutral transfer principle.

formativeAssessment: Maps each idea to its speaker.
Interprets death as advice from evidence.
Uses reporting verbs and whoever / a person who accurately.
expectedResponses: Heart and intellect must support one another for a person to reach salvation, and remembering death is presented as advice toward a meaningful and honest life, supported by the saying of the Prophet (pbuh).
content.transferTask: Write one practical time-management decision that reflects limited time without using fear language.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners handle the sensitive theme calmly and keep the three voices distinct?

classroomManagement.instructions: Lesson 1: In pairs, highlight the voices in three colors. Then check with the class using the signals: highlights that, according to him, as … said, quotation marks.
checkQuestions: How many colors? (three)
Which signals do we check? (highlights that, according to him, as … said, quotation marks)
classroomManagement.monitoring: Check that each idea is mapped to its speaker. Make sure death is read as advice, not a threat. In Lesson 2, listen for reporting verbs and whoever.

exitTicket: Write one attributed sentence (He believes that …) and one “Whoever …” sentence about learning.

rubricLevels.secure: Maps each idea to its speaker.
Reads the advice about death from the evidence.
Uses reporting verbs, whoever and a person who.
Applies the advice safely.

objectives: Define morality through both building virtues and giving up harmful habits.
Classify the principles and bad habits named in the chapter.
Interpret the greed/prison image as figurative.
Notice nouns for principles and adjectives for habits, and use is about + -ing, such as, teach + person + to and not only … but also.
content.pedagogy: Use a build / avoid / action table. Learners sort the named principles and bad habits, then notice something about the words themselves: principles are nouns (honesty, patience), habits are adjectives after “being” (arrogant, greedy). Word families (generous → generosity, humble → humility) make the pattern memorable. The poem is read as a figurative moral image.
priorKnowledge: Nouns and adjectives; examples with such as; gerunds after prepositions.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Morality is not only avoiding bad habits, and the greed/prison image is figurative rather than a literal event.
content.grammarFocus:

objectives: Synthesise the patience lines and the warning about rage and arrogance.
Explain patience as active self-control rather than passive inaction.
Identify Risalat al-Nushiyya and Divan as the two named works.
Use general statements (Those who … will …, Whoever …, If …, one must …) and verse-linking language in a final synthesis.
content.pedagogy: Treat the final chapter as a synthesis. Lesson 1 compares the patience lines with the anger line and secures the two named works. Lesson 2 shows learners how the poems turn an observation into a general principle (Those who …, Whoever …, one must …) and how the writer introduces verses and brings them into the present (In another verse, warns against, still, as follows).
priorKnowledge: Values and figurative language from Chapters 10–12; if-clauses; future with will.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Patience is not passive inaction; the chapter names two works, and its legacy claim is moral and literary, not military or political.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: general principles in poetry (Those who … will …, Whoever …, If …, one must …) · impersonal “one” = any person · linking verses (In another verse, warn against, still, as follows).
Notice (Activities 1–2): learners match five poem lines with their meanings, then decide who “one” refers to in “If faith is required, one must give up rage”.
Build (Activity 3): Complete the linking lines with In / against / still / follows.
Likely errors: *At another verse · *warns about against · *as following.
Use (Activity 4): a five-sentence principle-and-result paragraph using “Whoever …” or “If …, one must …”.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Read each line as two meaning units with a pause at the comma: “WHOever is FILLED with ANger | LOSes their FAITH”.
Contrast patience and rage with stress, not drama: “PAtience … RAGE”.
Titles: Ri-SA-le-tün Nus-HI-ye, di-VAN.
Word focus: PA-tience (/ʃ/), pos-SESS-es (three syllables), ev-er-LAST-ing, AR-ro-gance.
beforeReading: Ask learners to predict how a final chapter might connect virtues, poems, works and legacy.
duringReading: Mark the patience lines and their stated results.
Mark the rage/arrogance warning.
Box both named works.
Underline the final legacy statement.
afterReading: Lesson 1: complete the Quick Challenge and leave a bridge chart: patience / rage / works / legacy.
Lesson 2: Language Focus on general principles, “one” and verse-linking language.
Write a connected final profile of Yunus with at least two pieces of chapter evidence and one realistic patience or anger-control action.
content.lessonPlan: Lesson 1 (40 min): 0–5 Predict: What might a final chapter bring together?; 5–15 Listen to the poems and read; 15–25 Poem stations in groups: Each group gets one verse card, writes its meaning in plain English and one real-life example, then rotates once; 25–31 Patience vs rage comparison on the board with quoted evidence; 31–35 Works and legacy check: Name both works and the “still valuable today” claim; 35–38 Quick Challenge; 38–40 Bridge chart; Lesson 2 (40 min): 0–4 Retrieve the bridge chart; 4–14 Language Focus Activities 1–2 (the meaning of each line, then who “one” is); 14–20 Activity 3, then learners rewrite one line with “you” (If you want to keep your faith, you must …); 20–32 Use: Final synthesis paragraph about Yunus (who he was, two principles with evidence, the two works, why he is still valuable today); 32–38 Pairs read and give one piece of feedback with the rubric; 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: What results are attached to patience?
How is rage presented as a warning?
What evidence supports Yunus’s continuing moral and literary legacy?
interactiveTips: Use the Lasting Value and Patience hotspots as evidence, not as material for dramatic recitation.
Keep the two named works visible during the final synthesis.
Do not expand the legacy into political or military claims absent from the chapter.

metadata.title: Yunus Emre B1 Teacher Guide
metadata.subtitle: TYMM-aligned guide with chapter-specific support, inductive grammar and 40-minute lesson plans
metadata.estimatedDuration: 13 chapter units: Chapters 1–3, 7, 9 and 12 are planned for 40 minutes; Chapters 4–6, 8, 10–11 and 13 are planned as 40 + 40 minutes. Whole-book review pages follow separately.
metadata.targetAudience: B1 English learners, especially upper-secondary students.
metadata.targetLearners: Learners who can follow connected historical, biographical, conceptual and poetic texts and produce supported explanations and reflections.
metadata.purpose: Develop evidence-based B1 reading, listening, speaking and writing through Yunus Emre’s historical setting, Sufi thought, poetry and moral teaching, using the Language Focus attached to every story chapter.
metadata.approachDesc: Every story chapter follows the TYMM route. YDAB1 listening and YDAB2 reading establish meaning and evidence; the Quick Challenge checks comprehension. Grammar is then learned inductively, as the Maarif Model expects for English: in the Language Focus, learners first NOTICE a form in a real chapter sentence and work out what it does (the rule is confirmed only afterwards), then BUILD it in controlled, meaningful practice, and finally USE it in connected YDAB3 speaking and YDAB4 writing about their own world. Longer or denser chapters are divided into two 40-minute lessons rather than compressed. See https://tymm.meb.gov.tr/beceriler/yabanci-dil-alan-becerileri.
metadata.assessmentEvidence: 13 Quick Challenges, text-evidence checks, chapter Language Focus tasks and production/reflection, exit tickets, Knowledge Check, Vocabulary Challenge, Language Review, and Final Challenge.

formative: Language Focus: Noticing and controlled practice

readingFramework.before: Activate only what the chapter needs, with a short chapter-specific prediction, image, question or card task.
readingFramework.during: Listen first for gist, then read and follow the chapter’s own evidence structure: definition, source stance, cause chain, sequence, voice, image, generalisation or consequence.
readingFramework.after: Complete the Quick Challenge, then the chapter’s Language Focus (notice → build → use), then a connected B1 transfer about the learners’ own world. In 40 + 40 chapters, Lesson 1 secures meaning and evidence and Lesson 2 develops language and production.

vocabularyApproach.selection: Prioritise chapter Word Notes and the analytical words needed for the chapter’s key relationship.
vocabularyApproach.method: Infer meaning from context, image or audio before any direct explanation.
vocabularyApproach.recycling: Reuse vocabulary in Language Focus production, exit tickets and the cumulative review.

metadata.grammarApproach: Inductive and text-based. Start from the story sentence, ask a meaning question (What does this form tell us?), let learners formulate the rule in their own words, then confirm it and practise it in context. Rule explanations appear in the app only after learners answer. Do not replace the chapter work with unrelated grammar drills.
grammarSequence: Ch1: aim + method (by + -ing); parallel -ing list; in addition to + -ing; is known as
Ch2: due to; neither … nor …; still; source stance (according to, some sources say, around); was taught
Ch3: adding vs cause-result; while + past continuous passive; cope with
Ch4: If we …, we can …; the most …; however; where-clause; caused … to; failure to … worsened
Ch5: believed … would; because vs because of; however; caused; thus; -ing result clause
Ch6: passive focus; in time … became; almost like; began to be + past participle; made … poorer
Ch7: comes from vs was also inspired by; parallel past continuous; among; help + person + verb; during; under … pressure
Ch8: key-phrase meaning; which means; according to; so; only one / nothing … except
Ch9: text cohesion; should for duty; the most important; those who … also …
Ch10: figurative phrases; where … is absent; that is; describe … as; that-clause; not only … but also
Ch11: voices in a text; reporting verbs; for + person + to; whoever / a person who
Ch12: noun vs adjective; is about + -ing; such as; teach … to; not only … but also
Ch13: general principles in poetry; impersonal “one”; linking verses (in another verse, warn against, still, as follows)

skillsFocus.listening: TYMM YDAB1: follow narration and explanation for gist, relationships, voice and key details.
skillsFocus.reading: TYMM YDAB2: identify main ideas, direct evidence, source qualification, cause-result chains, contrast, figurative language and generalisation.
skillsFocus.speaking: TYMM YDAB3: explain relationships, compare ideas, attribute viewpoints, justify claims and transfer chapter language respectfully.
skillsFocus.writing: TYMM YDAB4: produce connected B1 paragraphs using evidence, source-safe wording, chapter patterns and short reflection.

valuesFocus: D5 Sensitivity — sensitivity to human consequences of conflict and behavior
D6 Honesty — source accuracy and honest interpretation
D10 Humility — humility and reduced attachment to status
D12 Patience — patience and disciplined self-control
D14 Respect — respectful treatment of people, beliefs and feelings
D16 Responsibility — responsible choices and use of limited time
D20 Helpfulness — generosity and community support
languageFocus: Every one of the 13 story chapters has an active Language Focus set built as notice → build → use.
Use Language Focus after basic comprehension and the Quick Challenge.
Always start from the story sentence: Ask what the form does before naming it.
Let learners answer first; the explanation shown after each answer confirms the rule they have found.
At B1 the last step is always connected production about the learners’ own world, not a retelling of the chapter.
For 40 + 40 chapters, use the second lesson for Language Focus and connected production rather than re-reading the whole story.
metadata.differentiationNotes: Reduce linguistic load without lowering the reasoning target: One evidence sentence at a time, selected vocabulary, audio replay, sentence frames and oral rehearsal. Extend by combining more chapter patterns or adding a second evidence relationship, not by introducing outside facts.

sensitiveNotes.title: Source fidelity and respectful discussion
notes: Keep theological explanations within the wording of the story.
Preserve qualifiers such as “some sources say”, approximate dates and attributed viewpoints.
Discuss war, captivity and death factually and without sensationalism; never role-play violence.
Treat poetic and heart/prison imagery as figurative where the chapter does.
Qur’anic references, prophetic sayings and poem lines are read, explained and matched to meanings; they are never gapped, “corrected” or rewritten.
Do not introduce legends, worksheets or biographical details absent from this B1 book.

globalCitizenship.title: Global Citizenship and Cultural Bridges
globalCitizenship.description: Yunus Emre’s story links a local Anatolian history with questions every community faces: How people are supported in hard times, how simple language can reach everyone, and how respect for each person’s heart shapes life together.

themes.title: Language that includes everyone:
themes.description: Yunus wrote in simple Turkish that many people could understand (Chapter 2). Discuss how clear language in public notices, science or school can include more people.

themes.title: Community support in hard times:
themes.description: Tekkes helped people and brought them together while Anatolia faced crisis (Chapter 3). Compare them with community centers, libraries or charities today, without claiming they solve every problem.

themes.title: The human cost of conflict:
themes.description: Chapters 5–6 show how war and dependence affected ordinary people. Discuss this factually and with sensitivity towards people affected by conflict today.

themes.title: Respect for every heart:
themes.description: The book describes breaking a heart as destroying Allah’s house (Chapter 10). Connect this with respectful speech at school and online.

actions: Rewrite one school notice in clearer, simpler English so that every student can understand it.
Find two community organisations in your area and write two sentences about what each one does.
Agree on three class rules for respectful speech, including online messages.

exitTicket: One idea from today’s chapter, with the sentence that supports it, is …
One language pattern I noticed today, and what it does in the sentence, is …
One action I can take this week that shows a value from the chapter is …

miniProject.title: A Guide in Simple Words
miniProject.desc: In groups, choose one principle from Chapters 12–13 (for example patience, honesty or controlling anger). Make a one-page poster or a short audio clip in clear English: Quote the line from the book, explain what it means, and give two realistic school examples. Use at least two Language Focus patterns such as “Whoever …” or “not only … but also …”.

reflectivePrompt.title: Patience and Kind Words
reflectivePrompt.desc: Yunus Emre describes breaking a heart as destroying Allah’s house, links patience with greatness and warns that whoever is filled with anger loses their faith. Write six to eight sentences about a time when patience or a kind word changed a difficult situation at school or at home. What did you do, and what happened as a result?

valuesEducation.title: TYMM Values in Action
valuesEducation.description: Use only values genuinely supported by the chapter. Require evidence first, then connect the value to an observable, age-appropriate action. See https://tymm.meb.gov.tr/beceriler/erdem-deger-eylem-cercevesi.

items.label: D6 Honesty
items.value: Source qualification, accurate attribution and honest interpretation are made visible in learners’ language.

items.label: D10 Humility / D12 Patience
items.value: Humility, patience and anger control are treated as observable habits rather than abstract labels.

items.label: D14 Respect / D5 Sensitivity
items.value: Respect and sensitivity guide discussion of people, belief, conflict, poetry and feelings.

items.label: D16 Responsibility / D20 Helpfulness
items.value: Responsibility and helpfulness connect ideas with realistic choices and community-support actions.

cefrProfile.intro: This book is written for CEFR B1. The table links the B1 descriptors of the End-of-Level Test B1 to the chapters of this book where learners practise them.

rows.descriptor: Can read straightforward factual texts on subjects related to his/her field and interest with a satisfactory level of comprehension.
practice: Chapter 12 (Morality and Good Habits): Sort every named principle and bad habit.
Whole book: Knowledge Check and Final Challenge.

rows.descriptor: Can write straightforward connected texts on a range of familiar subjects within his field of interest, by linking a series of shorter discrete elements into a linear sequence.
practice: Chapter 2 (His Language and Education): Write a five-sentence profile with one balanced evaluation, one approximate date and one attributed claim.
Chapter 10 (The Heart and Love): Write a paragraph explaining one respectful action and its effect on another person’s feelings.
