test.title: End-of-Level Test B1
test.when: Give the test when the class has finished the B1 books it reads this term. It has four parts and takes about 70 minutes plus a short speaking test for each learner.
parts: Reading and Language (45 minutes): in the app. The learner gets a test code at the end.
Writing (25 minutes): on paper. Write an article for your school website about a person you admire. (100–130 words)
Speaking (about 8 minutes): one learner with the teacher, in 2 parts.
Scoring: type the test code in “Score a test”, then score Writing and Speaking with the bands. Copy the pilot line for the pilot results sheet.

professionalDevelopment.intro: Use these steps to plan your own development with this book: a colleague observes one of two lessons, you keep a short log after each chapter, and you agree on scoring with colleagues before the End-of-Level Test.

peerObservation.focus: Contrast the strong Seljuk period with the later decline using chapter evidence.
lookFor: Instruction: Lesson 1: In groups of three, build a cause map with three cards. Label every arrow with a word from the text. Then compare maps in a gallery check and remove any arrow the text does not support.
Check questions: How many cause cards? (three) / What do you remove in the gallery check? (arrows the text does not support)

While learners work: Check that the graph shows the high point (1220–1237) and the decline after 1237. Make sure groups use two causes that work together. In Lesson 2, listen for the most … and however.
Evidence of “Chronology”: Keeps the chronology accurate.

peerObservation.focus: Keep worship/obedience and love of Creator and creation as distinct strands before connecting them.
lookFor: Instruction: Mark the chapter in two colors: goal and commands, and love. Then, in pairs, find one quoted sentence for each strand and one word that connects them.
Check questions: How many colors? (two) / What else do you find? (one word that connects them)
While learners work: Check that both strands are found. In Activity 1, ask learners to explain each link word on the strips. In the Use task, check Anyone who … should and Those who … also.
Evidence of “Two-strand evidence”: Gives evidence for both strands.

reflectionLog: After each chapter, answer the chapter’s “After the lesson” question in one or two sentences.
Write down the rubric criterion that most learners had not yet reached and the support you gave.
Every three or four chapters, look at the grammar sequence of this book and plan one short recycling activity for a form learners still avoid.
Before the End-of-Level Test, read your notes and choose two chapters to revise with the class.
standardisation: Before scoring, read the B1 descriptors for written and spoken production in the CEFR table of this book.

With a colleague, score the same three writing papers on your own with the B1 writing bands (Task, Organisation, Grammar, Vocabulary). Then compare and talk about any criterion where your scores differ by more than one band.
Score one speaking test together in the same way: both listen, both score, then compare.
Keep one agreed paper for each band as a sample for later scoring.

objectives: I can explain what a Sufi is and how the outer and inner sides of Islam are different.
I can explain why Yunus Emre is known as one of the founders of Turkish Sufi literature.
I can use by + -ing for a method and keep a list of principles parallel.
content.pedagogy: Read and listen for meaning, find the evidence, do the Quick Challenge, then use the chapter’s Language Focus in your own sentences.
content.grammarFocus: Decide what “by following Islamic mysticism” tells you (the method, not the reason), fix three forms so that the list stays parallel (giving, not attaching, In addition to being), then say the same aim, contribution and reputation another way: Follows Islamic mysticism to get closer, words which helped, People know him as.

content.lessonPlan: Before you read, look at the two hotspots. Which moral principles do you expect a Sufi to follow? Listen once for the main idea: Who was Yunus Emre? Read paragraph 2 again and number the moral principles in the list.
discussionPoints: Sufis give generously without expecting anything in return and respond to evil with kindness. Which of the two is harder for you, and what small step could you take this week?

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Go back to paragraph 3. Find “one of the first to” and “helped develop”. Choose the option that joins both ideas, then try again.

Paragraph 3: find the two roles of Yunus Emre and how people know him today.

objectives: I can explain why people love Yunus Emre’s works.
I can compare what he learned at the madrasa and at the tekke.
I can report history carefully with according to, around and “Some sources say that …”.
content.pedagogy: Read and listen for meaning, find the evidence, do the Quick Challenge, then use the chapter’s Language Focus in your own sentences.
content.grammarFocus: Match phrases such as “due to his style” and “neither too simple nor too complex” with their plain meanings, choose According to, around and say to report history carefully, then complete the tekke sentence with also, which and taught.
content.pronunciationFocus: Stress: MAD-ra-sa, TEK-ke, PHI-los-o-phy, lit-er-AR-y (or LIT-rer-y). Say the dates as ranges: Twelve forty to twelve forty-one, thirteen twenty to thirteen twenty-one.
content.lessonPlan: Look at the Simple Language hotspot. Can a text be simple and still have high literary quality? Listen once for the main idea: Why do people love his works? Read paragraph 2 again and underline every word that shows where information comes from or how exact it is.
discussionPoints: His works combine great literary quality with simple language. Think of a teacher or writer who explains hard ideas simply. What do they do that helps you understand?

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Go back to the end of paragraph 2. Read the sentence about the madrasa, then the sentence that begins “But he also studied”. Decide which place goes with which kind of learning, then try again.

whatToNotice: Paragraph 1 is about his style and gives reasons; paragraph 2 is about his life and education and gives sources.

readListen: Look at the Simple Language hotspot. Can a text be simple and still have high literary quality?
Listen once for the main idea: Why do people love his works?
Read paragraph 2 again and underline every word that shows where information comes from or how exact it is.

findAnswerInStory: Paragraph 1: find the reason for his popularity in the sentence with because.
Paragraph 1: find the sentence that places his style between two extremes.
Paragraph 2: find who lived in the same era, his dates, and the two places where he studied.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: plain, era, sources, tutor.
“This plain language helps people understand his writings and sayings easily.” What does plain language make possible?
Write one sentence with era about a period of history you know, and one sentence with sources.
content.quickChallengeGuide: The statement is about what he studied and where. Read the last two sentences of paragraph 2 and compare the two places.

metadata.title: Yunus Emre B1 — Self-Study Guide
metadata.subtitle: Read • Find • Check • Build • Use
metadata.estimatedStudyTime: About 25 minutes per chapter, plus the review pages at the end
metadata.whoIsThisFor: B1 learners who study the life, times and poems of Yunus Emre on their own or at home.
learningGoals: Understand the 13 chapters of Yunus Emre: History, Poetry, and Moral Thought.
Find evidence in the story before answering.
Explain causes, contrasts and results, and report views and sources carefully.
Use each chapter’s Language Focus in connected sentences.
Connect humility, love, patience and good habits with real actions.
recommendedUse: Study one chapter at a time.
Listen and read before the Quick Challenge.
Repair wrong answers with the text.
Do the Language Focus after you understand the chapter.
Do the review pages after Chapter 13.

sections.title: 1. One Chapter per Session
sections.text: Each chapter takes about 25 minutes. Open “Study Path” for the steps of your chapter.
points: Preview the title and hotspots.
Listen and read for the main idea.
Find the evidence.
Do the Quick Challenge.
Do the Language Focus.

sections.title: 2. Listen and Read
sections.text: Use the audio twice: Once for the main idea, once to follow the exact words. Many chapters include a poem; listen to how each line is read.
points: First listening: What is the chapter about?
Second listening: Follow the text line by line.
Replay one long sentence or one poem line and say it with the same pauses.

sections.title: 3. Word Notes and Hotspots
sections.text: Each chapter has four Word Notes and two picture hotspots. Use them after you have tried to understand the sentence yourself.
points: Guess the meaning from the sentence.
Check the Word Note.
Write the word in a new sentence of your own.

sections.title: 4. Quick Challenge
sections.text: Answer before you read the feedback. If you are wrong, repair the answer with the text.
points: Find the paragraph or the poem the question is about.
Read the key sentence again.
Explain why the right answer is right, then try again.

sections.title: 5. Language Focus
sections.text: Each chapter has four Language Focus activities built from the chapter’s own sentences.
points: Activity 1 (Notice): Look at a sentence and what it means.
Activities 2–3 (Build): choose, complete, correct or rewrite forms.
Activity 4 (Use): Write or say five to six connected sentences about a different situation.

sections.title: 6. When It Is Hard
sections.text: Change how you study, not your goal. Chapters 3 to 6 have many names and dates, and Chapters 8 to 11 have difficult ideas.
points: Work one paragraph at a time.
Use the hotspots to get the big picture first.
For history chapters, write a short timeline of names and dates.
For idea chapters, write each key idea in one sentence of your own.
Focus on two Word Notes today.

sections.title: 7. Values in the Story
sections.text: The book shows how Yunus Emre answered a very hard time with love, humility and good character. Connect each value to one action.
points: Humility: Do good without expecting anything in return, and do not chase wealth, status or fame (Chapter 1).
Care in hard times: Help people make sense of what is happening to them (Chapters 3 and 7).
Love and respect: Love of the Creator goes with love of the created, so do not break anyone’s heart (Chapters 9 and 10).
Heart and mind together: Think carefully and remember that time is limited (Chapter 11).
Good character: build honesty, patience and generosity, avoid greed, gossip and arrogance, and give up rage (Chapters 12 and 13).

sections.title: 8. At the End of the Book
sections.text: After Chapter 13, do the review pages in this order. Go back to the chapter when an answer is not clear.
